title: Shock in Deep Red Mississippi: Senate Race Hangs by a Thread in Potential Historic Upset
snippet: Democrat Scott Colom holds a paper-thin lead over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in a nail-biting Mississippi Senate race that could snap a 44-year GOP streak.
content:
JACKSON, Miss. — In what is shaping up to be the biggest shocker of the 2026 midterm elections, a U.S. Senate contest in deep-red Mississippi remains too close to call, threatening to end a four-decade Republican stranglehold on the seat.

As of Wednesday evening, Democratic challenger Scott Colom held a razor-thin lead of just 1,138 votes over incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. With 96% of the vote tallied, Colom leads with 49% to Hyde-Smith’s 48.9%. The Associated Press has held off on calling the race given the microscopic 0.1% margin.

If Colom’s lead holds, he would become the first Democrat to represent Mississippi in the U.S. Senate since 1982. He would also make history as the state's first Black U.S. Senator since the Reconstruction era.

A Broader Midterm Trend

The neck-and-neck contest comes amid a national wave of Democratic gains in the midterms, driven largely by public discontent over the economy, rising living costs, and foreign policy challenges under President Donald Trump. Democrats have already flipped seven Senate seats nationwide, including surprising pickups in conservative strongholds like Texas and South Carolina.

"It's unprecedented for Mississippi to be this competitive for Democrats, certainly in the last 40 years," said Aaron Hitefield, an assistant professor of political science at Mississippi State University. While Hitefield cautioned that the tight race doesn't necessarily mean Mississippi is turning into a battleground state overnight, he noted that low Republican turnout and voter dissatisfaction played a major role.

Missteps and Momentum

Political analysts point to starkly different campaign strategies as a key factor in the tight tally. Hyde-Smith faced backlash earlier this year after making comments about soaring grocery prices that voters viewed as out of touch, telling an interviewer that consumers had "so many proteins to choose from" when asked about rising beef costs. Colom’s campaign capitalized on the gaffe, running a viral ad campaign that resonated widely across the state.

Furthermore, Hyde-Smith ran a low-profile campaign, making few public appearances outside a joint rally with President Trump shortly before Election Day. In contrast, Colom, a local district attorney, mobilized intense grassroots enthusiasm.

The Final Count Could Take Days

Voters and campaign staffers will likely have to wait several days before a definitive winner emerges. Under Mississippi election law, election officials have five business days after Election Day to process affidavit ballots and count mail-in ballots postmarked by Election Day.

"Because of the razor-thin margins we currently see, I don’t expect any results to be called before then," said Emily Ommundsen, a political science professor at the University of Mississippi.

Both campaigns expressed optimism while acknowledging the long wait ahead. Speaking to supporters, Colom noted that momentum was on his side, while Hyde-Smith assured her base that remaining uncounted precincts would keep her in Washington. For now, all eyes remain fixed on Jackson as the final ballots trickle in.
